No, not clearly. For a stablecoin it's usually the weaker default, because reach isn't the constraint. Peg stability is, and that depends on deep liquidity and reliable redemption on every chain you're live on.

Twelve simultaneous launches split your initial liquidity into twelve thin pools. Thin pools are easy to push off peg, and an early depeg on any chain damages trust in the whole asset. Each chain also adds its own audit surface, bridge or messaging risk, oracle and monitoring needs, market-maker relationships, and possibly compliance work. A single exploit or mispriced pool on a minor chain can hit your reputation everywhere.

The usual stronger path is to launch on one to three chains where your target users and liquidity already are, prove the peg and redemption flow under real volume, then expand in waves. Build on a cross-chain token standard from day one (native burn-and-mint rather than wrapped or lock-and-mint, or something like xERC20) so adding chains later is cheap and doesn't create fragmented, non-fungible versions of your token.

A wide launch can make sense if you already have committed liquidity per chain (market makers, incentives budget, or partner integrations), the team and tooling to monitor all twelve, and distribution deals that need those specific chains on day one. If that's your situation, say so and the answer changes. Without it, "maximize reach" at launch tends to mean maximizing the number of places you can fail.
